# Optical gain and the erbium-doped fiber amplifier {#sec-edfa} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/edfa.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 22–24 (absorption and emission cross sections, optical gain coefficient), 25–42 (the EDFA: energy levels, cross sections, configurations, gain versus pump power, fiber length and output power, power conversion efficiency, pump length, worked example, gain equalisation) and 43–44 (noise figure, ASE).* ## Key relations An ion in the lower level absorbs a fraction of the light that crosses it, as if it presented an opaque area, the **absorption cross section** $\sigma_{ab}$ (slide 22). An ion in the upper level adds stimulated photons with an **emission cross section** $\sigma_{em}$ (slide 23). In a slab of thickness $\delta x$, with $N_1$ and $N_2$ ions per unit volume, the intensity changes by $\delta I/I=(\sigma_{em}N_2-\sigma_{ab}N_1)\delta x$. This defines the **optical gain coefficient** (slide 24), $$ g(\nu)=\sigma_{em}(\nu)N_2-\sigma_{ab}(\nu)N_1,\qquad G=\frac{P_\text{out}}{P_\text{in}}=\exp(gL). $$ In the EDFA (slides 25–28), Er³⁺ ions in silica glass absorb a 980 nm pump into the $^4I_{11/2}$ level, which decays in microseconds to the metastable $^4I_{13/2}$ level ($\tau_{sp}\approx10$ ms). Signals in the C band (1530–1565 nm) are amplified by stimulated emission back to the ground state $^4I_{15/2}$. Each level is split into a manifold of Stark sublevels, so $\sigma_{ab}(\lambda)$ and $\sigma_{em}(\lambda)$ are broad and different: absorption dominates at short wavelengths, emission at long ones (slide 28a). With the fractional inversion $x=N_2/N_0$ (slide 39), $$ g=\left[\sigma_{em}x-\sigma_{ab}(1-x)\right]N_0 . $$ Energy conservation bounds the output (slides 36–37). The **power conversion efficiency** $\eta_\text{PCE}=(P_{s,\text{out}}-P_{s,\text{in}})/P_{p,\text{in}}$ cannot exceed $\lambda_p/\lambda_s$ (one signal photon per pump photon at best), so $$ G=1+\eta_\text{PCE}\frac{P_{p,\text{in}}}{P_{s,\text{in}}},\qquad P_{s,\text{in}}<\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_s}\,\frac{P_{p,\text{in}}}{G-1}. $$ The pump is absorbed as it travels. It can keep all the ions in a length $L_p$ inverted only if it delivers $N_0h\nu_p$ per unit volume every $\tau_{sp}$ (slide 38): $\Gamma P_p\approx AN_0h\nu_pL_p/\tau_{sp}$, with $\Gamma$ the fraction of pump power that overlaps the doped core. ## Cross sections and gain spectrum (slides 28, 39–40) The cross sections below are a model shaped after Pedersen *et al.* (slide 28) and scaled to the slide-39 values at 1550 nm ($\sigma_{em}=3.2\times10^{-21}$ cm², $\sigma_{ab}=2.4\times10^{-21}$ cm²). Absorption and emission are linked by the McCumber relation, $\sigma_{ab}/\sigma_{em}=\exp[(h\nu-\varepsilon)/k_BT]$. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {erCross, edfaPropagate} from "./laser_sim.js" viewof gs = Inputs.form({ x: Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.7, step: 0.01, label: "fractional inversion x = N₂/N₀"}), N0: Inputs.range([0.1, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Er³⁺ concentration N₀ (10¹⁹ cm⁻³)"}), L: Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {value: 3, step: 0.1, label: "fiber length L (m)"}), G: Inputs.range([0.2, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "signal confinement factor Γ_s"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false gsOut = { const cs = [], gain = [], N0 = gs.N0*1e25; for (let i = 0; i <= 300; i++) { const w = 1450 + 170*i/300, [a, e] = erCross(w*1e-9); cs.push({w, s: a*1e25, who: "σ_ab"}, {w, s: e*1e25, who: "σ_em"}); const g = gs.G*(e*gs.x - a*(1 - gs.x))*N0; gain.push({w, GdB: 10*Math.log10(Math.E)*g*gs.L, g}); } const [a, e] = erCross(1550e-9), g1550 = gs.G*(e*gs.x - a*(1 - gs.x))*N0; const pk = gain.reduce((m, d) => d.GdB > m.GdB ? d : m, gain[0]); return {cs, gain, g1550, pk, xtr: a/(a + e)}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 220, x: {label: "wavelength (nm)"}, y: {label: "cross section (10⁻²¹ cm²)", grid: true}, color: {legend: true, range: ["#eb6834", "#2a78d6"]}, marks: [Plot.line(gsOut.cs, {x: "w", y: "s", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleX([1550], {stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "3,3"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 260, x: {label: "wavelength (nm)"}, y: {label: "gain G = 10 log₁₀ e^{gL} (dB)", grid: true}, marks: [Plot.areaY(gsOut.gain, {x: "w", y: "GdB", fill: "#1baf7a", fillOpacity: 0.25}), Plot.line(gsOut.gain, {x: "w", y: "GdB", stroke: "#1baf7a", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#0b0b0b"}), Plot.rectX([{a: 1530, b: 1565}], {x1: "a", x2: "b", fill: "#eda100", fillOpacity: 0.08})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
at 1550 nm: g = ${gsOut.g1550.toFixed(2)} m⁻¹, G = ${(4.343*gsOut.g1550*gs.L).toFixed(1)} dB · peak gain ${gsOut.pk.GdB.toFixed(1)} dB at ${gsOut.pk.w.toFixed(1)} nm · transparency at 1550 nm needs x = ${gsOut.xtr.toFixed(3)} (shaded: C band)
` ``` Lower the inversion: the short-wavelength side (1530 nm) turns from gain to loss first, because there $\sigma_{ab}>\sigma_{em}$. A partially inverted fiber amplifies long wavelengths only. This is how **L-band** amplifiers (1570–1610 nm) work: long fibers with a low average inversion. ### Worked example (slides 39–40), recomputed > A 3 m EDFA, core diameter 5 µm, $N_0=10^{19}$ cm⁻³, $\tau_{sp}=10$ ms, pumped with 25 mW at 980 nm, $\Gamma=0.7$. Find the > length that absorbs the pump, and the small-signal gain at 1550 nm for 100 % and 90 % inversion. ::: {#tbl-edfa-example .cell tbl-cap='The EDFA example of slides 39–40 recomputed. The slide also quotes 19.8 dB at 70 % inversion.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} A = np.pi*(2.5e-6)**2; N0 = 1e19*lz.CM3; hvp = lz.h*lz.c0/980e-9 Lp = 0.7*25e-3*10e-3/(A*N0*hvp) rows = [{"quantity": "pump photon energy", "value": f"{hvp/lz.qe:.3f} eV ({hvp:.3e} J)", "slide": "1.27 eV"}, {"quantity": "pump absorption length L_p = ΓP_pτ/(AN₀hν_p)", "value": f"{Lp:.2f} m", "slide": "4.4 m"}] for x, ref in ((1.0, "3.2 m⁻¹, 41.7 dB"), (0.9, "2.64 m⁻¹, 34.4 dB"), (0.7, "19.8 dB")): g, G = lz.edfa_gain_uniform(x, 3.2e-21*lz.CM2, 2.4e-21*lz.CM2, N0, 3.0) rows.append({"quantity": f"x = {x:.0%}: g, G", "value": f"{g:.2f} m⁻¹, G = {G:,.0f} = {lz.dB(G):.1f} dB", "slide": ref}) pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The slide's warning holds: losing 10 % of the inversion costs 7 dB of gain, because the 10 % of ions left in the ground state **absorb**. The small-signal gain at full inversion (41.7 dB) is an upper bound that is never reached. ## The EDFA along the fiber The uniform-inversion model ignores that the pump weakens along the fiber. The panel solves the steady-state two-level rate equations at every point. The local inversion is set by the local pump and signal photon fluxes, $$ x(z)=\frac{\sigma_{ab,p}\Phi_p+\sigma_{ab,s}\Phi_s}{(\sigma_{ab,p}+\sigma_{em,p})\Phi_p+(\sigma_{ab,s}+\sigma_{em,s})\Phi_s+1/\tau_{sp}}, \qquad \Phi_k=\frac{\Gamma_kP_k}{h\nu_kA}, $$ and each power grows or decays as $dP_k/dz=\Gamma_k[\sigma_{em,k}x-\sigma_{ab,k}(1-x)]N_0P_k$ (forward pumping, no ASE). ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof ed = Inputs.form({ Pp: Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: 25, step: 1, label: "pump power P_p (mW, 980 nm)"}), Ps: Inputs.range([-40, 10], {value: -30, step: 1, label: "input signal P_s,in (dBm)"}), ws: Inputs.range([1520, 1600], {value: 1550, step: 1, label: "signal wavelength (nm)"}), L: Inputs.range([1, 40], {value: 12, step: 0.5, label: "fiber length shown (m)"}), N0: Inputs.range([0.1, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "N₀ (10¹⁹ cm⁻³)"}), core: Inputs.range([2, 8], {value: 5, step: 0.1, label: "doped core diameter (µm)"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false edOut = { const Ps0 = 1e-3*10 ** (ed.Ps/10); const r = edfaPropagate({L: ed.L, Pp0: ed.Pp*1e-3, Ps0, wls: ed.ws*1e-9, N0: ed.N0*1e25, core: ed.core*1e-6, nz: 400}); const rows = r.flatMap(d => [{z: d.z, v: 10*Math.log10(Math.max(d.Pp, 1e-12)/1e-3), who: "pump (dBm)"}, {z: d.z, v: 10*Math.log10(Math.max(d.Ps, 1e-12)/1e-3), who: "signal (dBm)"}]); const G = r.map(d => ({z: d.z, G: 10*Math.log10(d.Ps/Ps0), x: d.x})); const best = G.reduce((m, d) => d.G > m.G ? d : m, G[0]), end = r[r.length - 1]; const pce = (end.Ps - Ps0)/(ed.Pp*1e-3), bound = 980/ed.ws; return {rows, G, best, end, Ps0, pce, bound}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 260, x: {label: "position z (m)"}, y: {label: "power (dBm)", grid: true}, color: {legend: true, range: ["#eb6834", "#2a78d6"]}, marks: [Plot.line(edOut.rows, {x: "z", y: "v", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 220, x: {label: "position z (m) = fiber length if cut here"}, y: {label: "gain (dB) / inversion × 40", grid: true}, marks: [Plot.line(edOut.G, {x: "z", y: "G", stroke: "#1baf7a", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.line(edOut.G, {x: "z", y: d => 40*d.x, stroke: "#4a3aa7", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}), Plot.dot([edOut.best], {x: "z", y: "G", r: 5, fill: "#e34948"}), Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#0b0b0b"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
gain at z = ${ed.L} m: ${(10*Math.log10(edOut.end.Ps/edOut.Ps0)).toFixed(1)} dB, output ${(10*Math.log10(edOut.end.Ps/1e-3)).toFixed(1)} dBm, residual pump ${(edOut.end.Pp*1e3).toFixed(2)} mW · optimum length Lopt ≈ ${edOut.best.z.toFixed(1)} m (G = ${edOut.best.G.toFixed(1)} dB) · ηPCE = ${(100*edOut.pce).toFixed(1)} % (bound λp/λs = ${(100*edOut.bound).toFixed(0)} %) · purple dashed: inversion x(z) × 40
` ``` Things to try: * Raise the input signal to 0 dBm. The signal now **saturates** the amplifier: it depletes the inversion, the gain drops and the PCE approaches its quantum limit $\lambda_p/\lambda_s=63$ %. * With a weak pump (3 mW), the gain curve has a maximum: beyond $L_\text{opt}$ the pump is exhausted and the unpumped erbium **absorbs** the signal (slide 34). * Move the signal to 1530 nm: higher peak gain, but the optimum length is shorter. ### Reproducing slides 33–35 The curves of slides 33–35 come from fibers with a small core and a low Er concentration (Giles *et al.*). The model reproduces them qualitatively with a 2.5 µm doped core, $N_0=1.5\times10^{18}$ cm⁻³ and a 1531 nm signal: ::: {#cell-fig-edfa-curves .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} kw = dict(wl_s=1531e-9, N0=1.5e24, core_d=2.5e-6, Gp=0.8, Gs=0.7) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.8)) for Pp, c in zip((2e-3, 3e-3, 5e-3), lz.PALETTE): r = lz.edfa_propagate(45, Pp, 1e-6, nz=450, **kw) G = lz.dB(r["Ps"]/1e-6); i = np.argmax(G) ax[0].plot(r["z"], G, color=c, label=f"P_p = {Pp*1e3:.0f} mW") ax[0].annotate("", (r["z"][i], G[i]), (r["z"][i], G[i] + 6), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=c)) ax[0].set(xlabel="fiber length (m)", ylabel="gain (dB)", ylim=(-10, 40)); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8) Pps = np.linspace(0.2e-3, 10e-3, 30) for Lf, c in zip((19.9, 13.6), lz.PALETTE[3:]): Gp = [lz.dB(lz.edfa_propagate(Lf, P, 1e-6, nz=200, **kw)["Ps"][-1]/1e-6) for P in Pps] ax[1].plot(Pps*1e3, Gp, color=c, label=f"L = {Lf} m") ax[1].set(xlabel="launched pump power (mW)", ylabel="gain (dB)"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8) Pin = np.logspace(-7, -2, 30) for Pp, c in zip((5e-3, 10e-3, 20e-3), lz.PALETTE): out = np.array([lz.edfa_propagate(25, Pp, P, nz=200, **kw)["Ps"][-1] for P in Pin]) ax[2].plot(lz.dB(out/1e-3), lz.dB(out/Pin), color=c, label=f"P_p = {Pp*1e3:.0f} mW") ax[2].set(xlabel="output signal power (dBm)", ylabel="gain (dB)"); ax[2].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Two-level EDFA model (2.5 µm doped core, N₀ = 1.5×10¹⁸ cm⁻³, Γ_p = 0.8, Γ_s = 0.7, τ = 10 ms, 980 nm pump, 1531 nm signal). Left: small-signal gain versus fiber length for three pump powers; the arrows mark the optimum length (slide 34). Centre: gain versus launched pump power for two lengths (slide 33). Right: gain versus output signal power, showing saturation (slide 35).](edfa_files/figure-html/fig-edfa-curves-output-1.png){#fig-edfa-curves width=1307 height=406} ::: ::: The saturation curves define the **saturated output power** quoted by manufacturers: the output at which the gain has dropped by 3 dB from its small-signal value (slide 35 notes). ## Gain flattening (slides 41–42) In a WDM system (Ch. 2) every channel crosses tens of amplifiers. A 1 dB gain difference per amplifier becomes 30 dB after 30 spans. Gain-flattened EDFAs combine a well-chosen average inversion with a passive filter (long-period or chirped fiber Bragg gratings, slides 41–42) whose loss is the mirror image of the gain: ::: {#cell-fig-flatten .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} wl = np.linspace(1520e-9, 1570e-9, 400) ab, em = lz.er_cross_sections(wl) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6)) for x in (0.55, 0.65, 0.75): g = 0.7*(em*x - ab*(1 - x))*1e25 ax[0].plot(wl*1e9, 4.343*g*3, label=f"x = {x}") x = 0.65; GdB = 4.343*0.7*(em*x - ab*(1 - x))*1e25*3 band = (wl > 1530e-9) & (wl < 1562e-9) filt = np.where(band, GdB - GdB[band].min(), np.nan) ax[0].axvspan(1530, 1562, color=lz.GRID, alpha=0.5, zorder=0) ax[0].set(xlabel="wavelength (nm)", ylabel="gain (dB)"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8) ax[1].plot(wl*1e9, -filt, color=lz.PALETTE[7], label="filter transmission (dB)") ax[1].plot(wl*1e9, np.where(band, GdB - filt, np.nan), color=lz.PALETTE[2], label="flattened gain (dB)") ax[1].set(xlabel="wavelength (nm)", ylabel="dB"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print(f"flattened gain {GdB[band].min():.1f} dB; filter must remove up to {np.nanmax(filt):.1f} dB") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Gain spectrum of the 3 m EDFA of slide 39 (N₀ = 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, Γ = 0.7) for three average inversions, and the loss filter that flattens the x = 0.65 curve to its minimum over 1530–1562 nm (a 'long-period grating' in the language of slide 42).](edfa_files/figure-html/fig-flatten-output-1.png){#fig-flatten width=1197 height=384} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` flattened gain 9.9 dB; filter must remove up to 3.5 dB ``` ::: ::: Flattening throws away the excess gain near 1530 nm. The price is pump power, and the flat shape holds only at one inversion, that is, at one total input power. Amplifiers in reconfigurable networks therefore control their gain electronically (automatic gain control) or add a variable attenuator. ## Going further: noise figure and amplified spontaneous emission (slides 43–44) {#sec-edfa-noise} Slide 43 defines the noise figure $\text{NF}=\text{SNR}_\text{in}/\text{SNR}_\text{out}$ but does not say where the noise comes from. Ions in the upper level also emit **spontaneously** into the guided mode. These photons are amplified like the signal, and form the broad **amplified spontaneous emission** (ASE) pedestal of slide 44a. In a bandwidth $B_o$ and two polarisations, the ASE power at the output is $$ P_\text{ASE}=2n_{sp}(G-1)h\nu B_o,\qquad n_{sp}=\frac{\sigma_{em}N_2}{\sigma_{em}N_2-\sigma_{ab}N_1}\ge1 . $$ The **spontaneous-emission factor** $n_{sp}$ equals 1 only at full inversion. When the amplified signal beats with the ASE on a photodiode (Ch. 5), the dominant noise is the **signal–spontaneous beat noise**, and $$ \text{NF}\approx2n_{sp}\frac{G-1}{G}+\frac1G\ \xrightarrow{G\gg1}\ 2n_{sp}\ \ge\ 2\ (3\text{ dB}). $$ No phase-insensitive amplifier can do better than 3 dB: amplifying a coherent state necessarily adds noise (Caves, 1982). ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof nf = Inputs.form({ x: Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 0.9, step: 0.005, label: "inversion x"}), ws: Inputs.range([1525, 1600], {value: 1550, step: 1, label: "signal wavelength (nm)"}), GdB: Inputs.range([5, 40], {value: 25, step: 0.5, label: "gain G (dB)"}), Bo: Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "optical bandwidth B_o (nm)"}) }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false nfOut = { const [a, e] = erCross(nf.ws*1e-9), nsp = e*nf.x/(e*nf.x - a*(1 - nf.x)), G = 10 ** (nf.GdB/10); const NF = 2*nsp*(G - 1)/G + 1/G, nu = 299792458/(nf.ws*1e-9), Bo = nu*nf.Bo/nf.ws; const Pase = 2*nsp*(G - 1)*6.62607015e-34*nu*Bo; return {nsp, NF, Pase, ok: e*nf.x > a*(1 - nf.x)}; } html`
${nfOut.ok ? html`nsp = ${nfOut.nsp.toFixed(3)} · NF = ${(10*Math.log10(nfOut.NF)).toFixed(2)} dB (quantum limit 3.01 dB) · PASE in ${nf.Bo} nm = ${(10*Math.log10(nfOut.Pase/1e-3)).toFixed(1)} dBm` : html`no gain at this wavelength and inversion: σemx < σab(1 − x)`}
` ``` The noise figure is lowest where the inversion is highest, which is at the **pump input end** of the fiber. This is why low-noise pre-amplifiers are forward pumped at 980 nm (full inversion possible) while booster amplifiers can be backward pumped or use 1480 nm pumps (higher PCE, but $x<1$ because the pump also stimulates emission). Slide 44b shows the other effect: when the input power rises, the signal saturates the inversion, $n_{sp}$ grows and the NF increases. ::: {#cell-fig-nf .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = np.linspace(0.6, 1, 200); G = 10**2.5 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6)) for w in (1530e-9, 1550e-9, 1565e-9): a, e = lz.er_cross_sections(w) nsp = lz.edfa_nsp(x, e, a) ax.plot(x, np.where(nsp > 0, lz.dB(lz.edfa_nf(G, nsp)), np.nan), label=f"{w*1e9:.0f} nm") ax.axhline(lz.dB(2), color=lz.INK2, ls="--", lw=1.2); ax.text(0.61, 3.2, "3 dB quantum limit", fontsize=8) ax.set(xlabel="inversion x = N₂/N₀", ylabel="NF (dB)", ylim=(2.5, 10)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Noise figure 2n_sp(G − 1)/G + 1/G of a 25 dB amplifier versus inversion at three signal wavelengths (model cross sections). At 1530 nm the absorption cross section is large, so incomplete inversion is penalised most.](edfa_files/figure-html/fig-nf-output-1.png){#fig-nf width=671 height=380} ::: ::: In a chain of amplifiers the noise figures add like those of electronic amplifiers (Friis): $\text{NF}_\text{tot}=\text{NF}_1+(\text{NF}_2-1)/G_1+\dots$ The first amplifier dominates, so it must have high gain and low NF. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Include the ASE in the model.** Add forward and backward ASE powers in bins of 1 nm to `edfa_propagate` (Giles–Desurvire model). The ASE depletes the inversion at high gain and limits the useful gain to about 40 dB. Solve the two-point boundary problem with `scipy.integrate.solve_bvp`. - **Pumping configurations** (slides 29–32). `edfa_propagate(..., backward_pump=True)` solves counter-propagating pumping. Compare the gain and the inversion at the input end (which sets the NF) for forward and backward pumping with the same pump power. - **Gain dynamics.** The 10 ms lifetime makes the EDFA gain too slow to follow individual bits at Gb/s: no pattern effects, unlike the SOA (@sec-soa). But adding or dropping WDM channels causes gain **transients** in the surviving channels within 10–100 µs. - **Other amplifiers.** Raman amplification uses the silica fiber itself (gain peak 13 THz below the pump, any band). Thulium (S band, 2 µm), praseodymium (O band) and bismuth-doped fibers cover other windows. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - E. Desurvire, *Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifiers: Principles and Applications* (Wiley, 1994; 2nd ed. 2002): the reference. - C. R. Giles and E. Desurvire, "Modeling erbium-doped fiber amplifiers", *J. Lightwave Technol.* 9, 271 (1991): the model used here, with ASE. - Kasap, sec. 4.3–4.4; Agrawal, *Fiber-Optic Communication Systems*, ch. 7 (optical amplifiers and their noise). ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Estimate the absorption coefficient of the unpumped fiber of slide 39 at 1530 nm and at 980 nm in dB/m. 2. With the along-fiber panel, find the minimum pump power that gives 20 dB at 1550 nm in 10 m. What is the PCE? 3. A booster EDFA must deliver +20 dBm from a 0 dBm input at 1550 nm. What pump power at 980 nm is needed at the very least? 4. Calculate the ASE power in 0.1 nm at the output of a 30 dB amplifier with NF = 5 dB. What is the OSNR for a 0 dBm output signal?
